projects.title: Bugwalk
projects.logline: Follow the click to the line that broke.
projects.brief: Bugwalk is an AI debug engineer. When a customer says something broke, it follows their visit to the exact line of code that was live, and opens the fix as a pull request for you to review.
projects.approach: One continuous take: the camera rides a single orange thread from a customer's failed checkout click, through her visit, into the failing line, and out as a pull request you merge.

story.challenge: Every debugging tool promises to find bugs faster. Bugwalk's real difference is the chain: from a customer's name to the request, the error, the version that was live and the pull request. The film had to show that chain unbroken in about 20 seconds.
story.audience: Small product teams who get "it broke" messages from customers and lose an afternoon tracing each one.
story.idea: Follow the click. One orange thread leaves the Pay button the moment checkout fails and never cuts away: it lights each row of the visit timeline, plugs into the line that failed, and that line flips into the fix.

scenes.title: Checkout broke
scenes.text: On a demo shop's checkout, a coupon is typed, Pay is clicked and an error appears. An orange thread leaves the button.

scenes.title: The visit
scenes.text: The camera follows the thread down into the customer's visit timeline, lighting each row until the red TypeError.

scenes.title: The line
scenes.text: The thread runs into the code window and plugs into total.ts line 84, marked "fails here".

scenes.title: The fix
scenes.text: On the drop, line 84 becomes a diff and the pull request opens with its title, why and where.

scenes.title: You decide
scenes.text: You decide when it merges: the camera pushes into Merge, one click, merged.

scenes.title: Same bug
scenes.text: The site's own comparison: 2 h 6 min by hand, then 11 min with Bugwalk.

scenes.title: Know why it broke
scenes.text: The logo, the trial button and bugwalk.app.

craft: The visit timeline, code window, diff and pull request panel are rebuilt from bugwalk.app's own product UI, so developers see the real flow.
The thread is drawn frame by frame as it travels, so the whole hunt reads as one shot without a single cut.
Bugwalk's palette from the site's CSS: paper #FBFAF7, ink #181612 and the orange #A54C00, in DM Sans.
A chill 90 BPM track ("Helios Tilt" by CM ONNI, CC BY) that builds through the hunt and lands its groove on the fix. 16:9, no voiceover.

projects.title: PeerPush
projects.brief: PeerPush is a product discovery platform for people and AI. Paste your URL, AI builds a structured profile of your product that assistants can read, and you launch it to 51,000+ builders.
projects.approach: A customer asks an AI for the best tool and you're not in the answer. The chat rewinds like tape, you list on PeerPush, and the exact same question now names you.

story.challenge: "Get found by AI" is a new and fuzzy promise. The film had to make founders feel the problem in one glance, then show the concrete thing PeerPush does about it: a profile written in words AI can read.
story.audience: Indie founders, makers and small SaaS teams who have shipped something and want to be found by people and by AI assistants.
story.idea: Ask the same question twice. The opening AI chat names two other tools; the chat rewinds like a tape into PeerPush, and after the listing goes live the identical chat replays with a new answer.

scenes.title: Not in the answer
scenes.text: A customer asks an AI chat for the best tool. It recommends two others.

scenes.title: Rewind
scenes.text: The chat rewinds like tape into PeerPush's own how-it-works page, and the cursor clicks Paste your URL.

scenes.title: Paste your URL
scenes.text: The URL is typed into step 1 and the camera pans to step 2 as AI builds the profile.

scenes.title: Words AI can read
scenes.text: The site's example profile fills the frame: who it's for, use cases, what it replaces, pricing, platforms, then Live.

scenes.title: Launch day
scenes.text: On the site's example launch board, the product climbs to the top. Launch to 51,000+ builders.

scenes.title: Same question
scenes.text: The identical chat replays, and this time the answer names the product.

scenes.title: Read by AI
scenes.text: The homepage's counter: read 32.8M times by 33 AI systems in the last 30 days.

craft: The how-it-works steps, example profile and launch board are rebuilt from peerpush.com's own pages and copy. Product names in the chats and on the board are PeerPush's own examples, labelled as examples on screen.
The rewind is the film's turn: the chat un-types in reverse through tape tracking bands, then plays again with a new ending.
PeerPush's look from the site's CSS: white, black and purple #9333EA, all in Geist.
A funk track ("Funk in my Pocket" by OptiKill, CC BY) with cuts on its real downbeats, a zip and riser on the rewind and stamps as profile rows land. 16:9, no voiceover.

projects.title: AdMiro
projects.logline: Somewhere in your ads, money is leaking.
projects.brief: AdMiro connects Google Ads and Meta Ads to the AI app you already use, Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, Codex and more. Ask how your ads are doing in plain words; it pulls the numbers and answers, and before it pauses a campaign or changes a budget it waits for your yes.
projects.approach: Tell it through one small-shop owner who runs her own ads: Maya at Northwind Outdoor, the demo business from AdMiro's own site. Her ad money becomes a swarm of moths flying out of two dashboards, and the AdMiro mark comes alive as Miro, who plugs both platforms into her AI chat and helps her catch them one question at a time.

story.challenge: An AI connector for ad accounts is easy to describe and hard to feel. The film had to make a busy owner recognise the late-night dashboard flipping in seconds, then show that the AI does the digging while every change still waits for her approval, without a voiceover.
story.audience: Owners of small online shops and small teams who run their own Google and Meta ads, already use an AI chat app, and have no time to live in two ad dashboards.
story.idea: Wasted spend as money moths. Each moth carries a dollar bill and the name of the campaign burning it. The AdMiro logo becomes a character whose little flag is a sign it holds up: a plug, a magnifier, a question mark while it waits for her yes, and a tick once she says it.

scenes.title: Money leaking
scenes.text: 9:47 PM in Maya's shop. She flips between the Google Ads and Meta Ads tabs while spend climbs and sales stay flat, and three money moths burst out of the screen, each labelled with its campaign.

scenes.title: Plugged in
scenes.text: The screen turns into her Claude chat. Miro hops onto the laptop and plugs in Google Ads and Meta Ads, both ticking green, under the site's own headline.

scenes.title: Plain words
scenes.text: Over the site's forest art, Maya types the hero's own question, "Anything on Google that spent money last week with no sales?" The answer lands and Miro traps that campaign's moth in a camping lantern.

scenes.title: Your yes
scenes.text: Claude asks before pausing. Miro holds up a question mark and taps its foot, the cursor clicks Yes, pause, the row turns Paused and the moth falls asleep.

scenes.title: Google vs Meta
scenes.text: In ChatGPT, "Where should next month's budget go?" Brand search and Instagram Reels land side by side, and Miro's balance scale settles towards the cheaper cost per sale.

scenes.title: Back to work
scenes.text: Next morning the moths sleep in the lantern and Maya waves from the counter. The site's closing card: "Check your ads in one question. Then get back to work." Start free gets a click.

craft: Maya, Miro, the money moths and the shop are drawn and animated in code, so the story is warm and specific without stock footage.
The Claude and ChatGPT windows, campaign rows, status pills, chips and Start free button are rebuilt from theadmiro.com's own markup and demo data, over the site's own forest illustrations.
Brand system lifted from the site's CSS: page #FAFAFB, ink #171717 and green #007F5F, in Figtree headlines and Inter text, with the logo mark turned into the hero character.

A light 100 BPM score in D major with every shot change on the beat, and tab clicks, typing, pops and a confirm chime on the yes mixed under the music. Laid out shot by shot for both 16:9 and 9:16. No voiceover.

projects.title: Young Growth Diagnostic
projects.logline: Posting. Campaigns. PR. Films. Events. So why is growth flat?
projects.brief: A free online Growth Readiness Diagnostic from Young, a Mumbai marketing agency: a short form, 22 questions across six growth levers, a score out of 90 that places the business in Stability, Success or Scale, a PDF report sent on WhatsApp and email, and a free 30-minute call with their growth experts.
projects.approach: Start with the founder's real problem: a screen full of finished marketing and a growth line that won't move. Then walk the viewer through the whole real funnel, from the site's hero to the report and the free call, and close on the brands Young has worked with and the agency's own call to action.

story.challenge: Agencies usually sell themselves with showreels and service lists. Young wanted to sell a diagnosis, not more activity, so the film had to make busy-but-flat founders recognise themselves in seconds and then understand exactly what happens after they click, without a voiceover.
story.audience: Founders and business leaders of established Indian companies whose marketing is busy but whose pipeline is unpredictable, and who are open to fixing the system rather than adding another campaign.
story.idea: Busy is not growing. Activity cards tick in as done, one per word, while the growth line beside them stays flat and turns red. An orange scan beam sweeps the screen like an X-ray, and the brand's circled-Y ring opens into every next step of the real funnel.

scenes.title: Busy, not growing
scenes.text: Reel posted, campaign live, press mention, brand film, event: every card ticks green while the business growth line stays flat and turns red.

scenes.title: The hero
scenes.text: The site's own hero, rebuilt: orange gradient, duotone portrait, "Your Business is Growing?" and the cream Diagnose My Growth System button, which gets a click.

scenes.title: The form
scenes.text: The real form fills at speed: years in business, revenue band, and "More qualified leads" picked from the actual priority list.

scenes.title: 22 questions
scenes.text: A glimpse of the real diagnostic: the live statements and its 1 to 5 scale, two answered on camera, three more flicking past, then "Our team is reviewing your growth system...".

scenes.title: The result
scenes.text: A score out of 90 lands in the Success band, six levers fill out of 15, and the camera pushes in as the leak turns red next to what is working.

scenes.title: The report
scenes.text: The PDF report arrives on WhatsApp and in the inbox, and its cover opens: Growth Readiness Diagnostic, prepared for the business, with its stage and score.

scenes.title: The free call
scenes.text: "Let us understand your business, not just your score." The three benefits stack in and Book My Free 30-Minute Expert Call gets pressed.

scenes.title: Four engines
scenes.text: Young, Youngagement, YFX Creations and youngXperiences rise in on the beat and are threaded into one circled Y: one accountable partner.

scenes.title: Brands worked with
scenes.text: Lodha, Tata, Raheja Realty, Saint-Gobain, The Times of India, Ekta World and the Filmfare Awards pop in as a logo wall.

scenes.title: Find the gap
scenes.text: The site's closing line, "Before You Add More Marketing, Find the Gap That Matters Most.", with the button pressed, the URL and the offer: free diagnostic, report on WhatsApp and email, free expert call.

craft: The landing page, form, questionnaire, result view and free-call section are rebuilt from the live site's markup, in the site's own Harabara display font, with every headline and question in the agency's words.
The report pages follow the design of Young's real PDF report, filled with a sample business and sample scores rather than any real client's data.
Revised with the client after the first cut to show the full funnel and the brands they have worked with, then laid out shot by shot for both 16:9 and 9:16.
A 120 BPM score in A minor that lifts at the reveal, with every shot change on the beat and ticks, clicks and a scan riser mixed under the music. No voiceover.

projects.title: FlavorLinq
projects.logline: Saturday, 8 PM. Table 4 still has no menu.
projects.brief: A QR digital-menu and restaurant OS: guests scan a table QR and get a web menu with no app, while owners edit prices, mark dishes out of stock, read feedback and see sales insights from one dashboard.
projects.approach: One Saturday night at a busy bistro, told by a cast of drawn characters: a waiter buried in paper menus, an owner reprinting them for one price change, and Amit at Table 4. Then FlavorLinq takes over, one real feature per beat, until the same night is calm.

story.challenge: Restaurant software usually gets sold with dashboards and feature lists. Busy owners need to feel the weekend rush they already live with, then see in seconds how each part of FlavorLinq takes it away, without a voiceover.
story.audience: Owners and managers of busy Indian restaurants and cafés who are tired of reprinting menus and chasing tables on a Saturday night, and want results without a long setup.
story.idea: Tell it as one night. The rush, the toppled tower of menus and a full reprint for a ₹20 price change set up the pain. Then the same guest, owner and chef show the scan, the live update, the feedback and the insights, and the film ends back in the same room: Saturday, 8 PM, sorted.

scenes.title: The rush
scenes.text: A packed bistro at night. The waiter sprints in with a wobbling tower of paper menus, three tables wave at him, and Table 4 still has nothing. The tower topples.

scenes.title: The reprint
scenes.text: In the back office the owner strikes ₹160 off the paper menu and scribbles ₹180, the printer starts spitting out a new stack, and she facepalms.

scenes.title: The reveal
scenes.text: The site hero, rebuilt: eyebrow pill, wordmark and "The Smart OS for Modern Dining.", with the QR table stand and phone menu dropping in.

scenes.title: Scan, no app
scenes.text: Amit points his phone at the table stand, the scan corners lock on, and the real web menu rises into frame and scrolls.

scenes.title: Live updates
scenes.text: The chef calls the Tandoori finished. The owner flips it to unavailable and changes a price, and Amit's menu updates on the spot.

scenes.title: Feedback
scenes.text: Amit rates spice, service and taste and types "Waah! Mast Biryani thi!". It lands on the owner's dashboard and she replies.

scenes.title: Insights
scenes.text: Scans tick up, Butter Chicken races Dal Makhani in the live chart, and average order value climbs 20% while the owner sips her chai.

scenes.title: Real owners
scenes.text: The site's testimonial cards, with a pull line from each of three restaurant owners and the "Reaching 50+ Venues" badge.

scenes.title: Sorted
scenes.text: The same bistro, now calm: QR stands on every table, guests browsing on their phones, the waiter carrying food. Start Free Trial gets a click.

craft: The waiter, owner, chef and guests, and the bistro itself, are drawn and animated in code, so the story feels warm and specific without stock footage.
The guest menu, Menu Management table, feedback screen and insights dashboard are rebuilt from the product's real screenshots, with the site's own copy, ₹ prices and dishes.
Brand system lifted from flavorlinq.com: slate #0F172A, ember orange #F97316 and amber, with the orange-to-peach headline gradient and pill eyebrows.
A warm 120 BPM score with every scene change on the beat, scan beeps, toggle clicks and printer whirr mixed under the music. No voiceover.

projects.title: TaskLoco
projects.logline: Sticky notes are great. Until the window is open.
projects.brief: A sticky-note to-do list and task manager: tasks, to-dos and calendar on one visual wall, with real alarms, tags, web clipping and sharing across web, iPhone, Android and Chrome.
projects.approach: Maya runs her whole life on paper Post-its until a breeze blows them off the wall and she misses a client call. Then we move her notes into the real TaskLoco app, one feature per beat, until the alarm rings on time.

story.challenge: TaskLoco's own site is busy, with many colours and a long feature list. The video had to pick the few things that matter to a sticky-note person and make each one land in seconds, without a voiceover.
story.audience: Visual thinkers who already cover their desk in Post-its, like freelancers, students, creators and small teams, who find heavier project tools too much and just want to see everything on one wall.
story.idea: Tell it as one afternoon. A freelance designer's wall of paper notes blows away and the "Call Sam 3 PM!" note slides behind the desk. She moves her notes into TaskLoco, and the same call comes back as an alarm that actually rings, five minutes early.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: A sunny desk and a wall of paper sticky notes. The window's open, the curtains billow and the notes start falling, one by one.

scenes.title: The miss
scenes.text: 3:14 PM. Notes all over the desk, a missed call from the client on the phone, and "Call Sam 3 PM!" lying right next to it.

scenes.title: The reveal
scenes.text: The TaskLoco roundel spins in and the fallen paper notes fly up and flip into app stickies.

scenes.title: Note, task, event
scenes.text: One sticky, typed, ticked and given a reminder, word for word from the site: it's a note, it's a task, it's an event.

scenes.title: The storyboard
scenes.text: The real board with its menu. One sticky turns red for urgent, then a #client filter clears the board in one go.

scenes.title: Clip the web
scenes.text: The Chrome extension popup saves a video as a sticky, with the video embedded, in a single click.

scenes.title: The alarm
scenes.text: 2:55 PM. The phone rings with the app's own alarm screen, and Maya calls Sam five minutes early.

scenes.title: Share
scenes.text: A sticky shared with a teammate in one tap. It lands on their board as their own copy.

scenes.title: Try it free
scenes.text: Paper notes drift down like confetti behind the logo, the site's headline and the Try it free button.

craft: Maya, her desk and the falling notes are drawn and animated in code, so the story could feel warm without stock footage.
The storyboard, the Chrome extension popup and the phone alarm are rebuilt from the app's real screenshots, and every feature line is the site's own copy.
A cleaner brand system than the site itself: cream paper, sticky yellow, plum and green, with Fredoka and Nunito taken from taskloco.com.
Cut to a bright 120 BPM score so every scene change lands on a bar, with paper rustles, ticks and an alarm ring under the music. No voiceover.

projects.title: Scan4Feedback
projects.logline: One QR code. Two very different outcomes.
projects.brief: A QR review tool for restaurants, cafés, hotels and clinics. Happy guests get routed to Google, unhappy ones to the owner's private inbox, and an AI-assisted review writes itself in the guest's language.
projects.approach: We built the guest's phone flow and the owner's dashboard from the live product's own UI, then cut the two outcomes side by side so the idea lands in one glance.

story.challenge: Scan4Feedback does two jobs at once. It gets happy guests to actually post a review, and it keeps unhappy ones off Google until the owner has heard them first. Both had to land in under a minute, with no voiceover, for owners scrolling between services.
story.audience: Owners and managers of Indian restaurants, cafés, hotels and clinics, from a single outlet to many branches, who live and die by their Google, Zomato and Swiggy rating.
story.idea: Open on the owner's pain: a busy Saturday kitchen, a one-star review dropping onto the screen and the rating ticking down while the happy table walks out without a word. Then show the fix twice, side by side. The same QR code sends a five-star guest to Google with the review already written, and a two-star guest to the owner's private inbox.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: Wok fire on a Saturday night. A one-star review slams in and the rating ticks from 4.6 to 4.3. Happy guests leave quietly; unhappy ones review you.

scenes.title: The reveal
scenes.text: The product's own hero footage of a guest scanning the table tent, with the logo and the site's headline: one QR code, two very different outcomes.

scenes.title: No app, nine languages
scenes.text: The table tent on the left, the guest's phone on the right. The rating screen switches from English to Hindi to Bengali before the guest taps the fifth star.

scenes.title: The review writes itself
scenes.text: The guest picks what stood out, chooses a warm tone and watches the review draft itself. They edit a line, copy it and paste it straight onto Google.

scenes.title: Two outcomes
scenes.text: Two phones side by side. Four and five stars go to Google, Zomato or Swiggy. One to three stars go to the owner, privately, and are never posted.

scenes.title: One dashboard
scenes.text: The owner's view: total scans, average rating, reviews routed to Google against feedback kept private, and every branch in one table.

scenes.title: The proof
scenes.text: The product's own numbers count up over close-up footage of stars being tapped, followed by a café owner's testimonial.

scenes.title: The plans
scenes.text: The pricing cards rise in, then a toggle flips to the organic-review plans. Start free for 15 days.

craft: Every screen is the live product. The guest flow and the owner dashboard were rebuilt from scan4feedback.com, with copy lifted word for word from its language files.
The language switch uses the app's real Hindi and Bengali strings, not placeholder text.
Cut to a 120 BPM score so every scene change lands on a bar, with sound effects on each tap. No voiceover, so it works muted in a feed.
Two masters from one edit: 16:9 for YouTube, LinkedIn and the website, 9:16 for Reels, Shorts and WhatsApp Status.

projects.title: Headel
projects.brief: A no-code store builder for social sellers: add products, get a shop link, share it on Instagram and WhatsApp, and get paid by UPI, card or net banking.
projects.approach: A relay story. The shop link is the hero: a home baker builds it, a buyer taps it, and it gets passed on to the next seller. The real builder UI carries every handoff.

story.challenge: Headel's real competitor isn't another store builder. It's the DM inbox. Social sellers already have followers who want to buy; what they don't have is a way to stop answering "price?" forty times a post. The film had to make one link feel like the whole shop, for sellers who have never built a website.
story.audience: Indian home businesses and resellers who sell through Instagram and WhatsApp DMs today: home bakers, sneaker resellers, thrift sellers, achaar makers.
story.idea: A relay where the shop link is the hero. Meher, a home baker, posts a cake and drowns in identical DMs. She builds her shop, a follower taps the link and pays, and then the link flies over the hill to a sneaker reseller, a thrift seller and a grandmother selling achaar, each on a different screen, until the whole cast stands under Headel's sky.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: Meher posts a cake and her phone erupts: "price?", "price??", "kitna?". The unread badge climbs to 99+.

scenes.title: The reveal
scenes.text: An iris out of her phone into Headel's own sky-blue hero: "Start selling online in minutes", and a click on Get Started.

scenes.title: Build the shop
scenes.text: Headel Admin: the cake photo drops in, a name and a price are typed, Save, and the product grid fills.

scenes.title: Her own link
scenes.text: Domain chips roll until "meherbakes" is typed, the address locks in with free SSL and goes straight into her bio.

scenes.title: A follower buys
scenes.text: Arjun taps the bio link, lands on the storefront, picks the cake and pays with UPI.

scenes.title: Paid
scenes.text: Back on Meher's phone: a New Order toast and a payout card, straight to her bank. She cheers.

scenes.title: The relay
scenes.text: The link flies over the hill to Kabir's sneakers, Zoya's thrift store and Nani's achaar, on phone, tablet and laptop.

scenes.title: One dashboard
scenes.text: Total sales count up, the bars grow and recent orders fill in, while Meher sips her chai.

scenes.title: Everything you need
scenes.text: A feature board on the sky. Eight cards pop in one by one while the cast peeks around the edges.

craft: The site hero, the admin dashboard, the storefront and the domain chips are rebuilt from headel.com's own design. Screens behind the login are recreated in the same system.
Five characters drawn in code, each a different kind of social seller, so every viewer finds the one that looks like them.
The site's statistics and testimonials are marked as fictional in its own footer, so none of them appear in the film.
Cut to a 120 BPM score across ten scenes in 58 seconds, with no voiceover.

projects.title: Lensmilk
projects.brief: An AI studio that turns one product brief into creator-style UGC ads, explainers and localised cuts.
projects.approach: Open on five finished ads slamming onto the screen, then show the flow from brief to master to every format, using the product's real screens.

story.challenge: Lensmilk makes ads. A promo for an AI ad studio has to clear a higher bar than most: it has to look like the work it promises, and prove that one brief really does turn into a batch of finished ads, in under 40 seconds.
story.audience: Performance marketers, DTC brands and agencies who need many UGC ad angles to test, quickly, without booking creators.
story.idea: Lead with the output, not the interface. Five finished UGC ads, all real Lensmilk renders, slap onto the screen in the first beat and none of them was shot. Then walk the pipeline one feature per shot: brief, hooks, cast, free sketch, master, every format, every language.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: Five real Lensmilk UGC ads land as 9:16 cards. Five UGC ads. Zero shoots.

scenes.title: The reveal
scenes.text: lensmilk.com's hero, rebuilt: "Start with UGC. Build beyond the ad."

scenes.title: UGC ad factory
scenes.text: A brief is typed into the studio and three hook cards come back: problem, proof and review.

scenes.title: Cast
scenes.text: A presenter grid: house talent, a custom avatar, or your own face with consent verified. Raw UGC or polished.

scenes.title: Preview free
scenes.text: The sketch board renders hook, proof and ask in seconds for zero credits, and gets an Approved stamp.

scenes.title: Engine routing
scenes.text: Each beat is routed to the best of 17 verified engines, and the master plays.

scenes.title: Every format
scenes.text: The master splits into 9:16, 1:1 and 16:9 cards labelled for TikTok, feeds, YouTube and Shorts.

scenes.title: Every language
scenes.text: The same ad re-voiced, with captions cycling through English, Spanish, French, German and Portuguese.

craft: Every ad on screen is Lensmilk's own proof-gallery output, not a mock-up.
The studio is behind sign-in, so it's rebuilt in the site's own design language: Space Grotesk, mono labels, hard ink shadows and red full stops.
One feature per shot, each with a numbered eyebrow, so a viewer can count the pipeline as it goes past.
Cut to 120 BPM with every shot starting on a beat. No voiceover.

projects.title: The Junction Café
projects.brief: A cosy neighbourhood café and restaurant in Belgharia, Kolkata, with a big menu in one small, warm room.
projects.approach: Built from the owner's own photos and menu: we start close on their wall sign, pull back to reveal the room, and end on the way there.

story.challenge: A neighbourhood café doesn't need a feature list. It needs people to walk in. The ad had to make a small room in Belgharia feel worth the trip, using only the owner's own photos and menu, in about 20 seconds.
story.audience: Locals in Belgharia and North Kolkata looking for a place to sit with coffee, snacks and a big menu.
story.idea: Start on the café's own wall sign, "Life Begins After Coffee", and finish the line for it: "…and it begins here." Then pull back to show the room, open the actual menu and end with a pin on the street map, so every shot points at the door.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: Tight on the orange wall sign, then a pull back to the tables and stools: "…and it begins here."

scenes.title: The reveal
scenes.text: The owner's photo of a cup pushes in as The Junction's logo, name and neighbourhood land on wood.

scenes.title: The menu
scenes.text: Their own menu page, wood and parchment. Eight real categories tick in on the beat while the menu's food art lands around it.

scenes.title: Bites and corners
scenes.text: The owner's photos as polaroids: crispy bites with dip, and the wall art. Crispy bites, cosy corners.

craft: Built entirely from the café's own material: the owner's photos, the menu PDF's logo, colours, textures and food art.
No customer photos from Google, and no prices, at the owner's request.
The menu's own slab and rounded fonts, matched with close free equivalents, so the ad feels like the café rather than a template.
Ends on a warm street map with a pin, the address and the Google rating, so viewers know exactly where to go.

projects.title: The MindMates
projects.brief: An AI wellbeing companion for students that remembers your journey across journals, mood logs, Worry Jars and breathing tools.
projects.approach: It's 1:47 AM before the boards, and a student's worries pop out as small anxious creatures. The companion's real UI calms them down one by one.

story.challenge: A wellbeing app for students can't sound like an ad, and it can't make light of stress either. The MindMates' real difference, that it remembers you, is also the hardest thing to show in a 40-second video with no voiceover.
story.audience: Indian school and college students facing exams, career choices and stress, and the schools and colleges that support them.
story.idea: It's 1:47 AM, the night before boards. Meera's worries pop out of her head as small, anxious creatures with labels. The MindMates logo comes alive as "the Mate" and catches them one at a time, one feature each, until every worry has a home and is fast asleep.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: 1:47 AM. Worries pop out of Meera's head on the beat: "Boards in 12 days", "Sleep: 4h", "Engineering or design?"

scenes.title: The reveal
scenes.text: Her phone lights up and the Mate springs out and waves. Every student deserves someone who understands them.

scenes.title: Worry Jar
scenes.text: She types "What if I'm not enough?" and drops it in. The worry flies into the jar and falls asleep.

scenes.title: Breathe
scenes.text: A guided breathing ring, grounded in CBT and DBT: breathe in, hold, breathe out.

scenes.title: Morning brief
scenes.text: Sunrise. Her Brief shows last night's sleep, a Physics mock on Thursday and what today needs.

scenes.title: It remembers
scenes.text: The site's own comparison: a goldfish of a generic AI says "How can I help?" while the Mate recalls last week.

scenes.title: One companion
scenes.text: The last worries settle into the four pillars: health, career, daily guidance and AI companion.

scenes.title: Privacy
scenes.text: Permission toggles, one switched off. Your information remains yours.

craft: Meera, the Mate and the worry creatures are all drawn and animated in code, so the story could be warm without using stock people.
Every line on screen is the site's own copy, and the comparison cards are rebuilt from themindmates.in.
The app isn't public yet, so its screens are recreated in the brand's own system: indigo, Playfair and soft paper.
A calmer 96 BPM score instead of the usual 120, with cuts on bars, to match the subject.

projects.title: ParkKolkata
projects.brief: A free community map of parking spots across Kolkata, with free, paid and verified spots shown before you arrive.
projects.approach: A yellow car circles the real Esplanade blocks on an OpenStreetMap base, then the app's search, filters and spot sheet park it.

story.challenge: ParkKolkata is a free community map with a simple job: tell drivers where they can park before they get there. The video had to make that feel urgent to anyone who has ever circled a block in central Kolkata, and walk through every feature in 30 seconds.
story.audience: Drivers and riders heading into Kolkata's busiest areas: Esplanade, New Market, Park Street.
story.idea: Esplanade, 6 PM. A small yellow car laps the real blocks while every kerb says FULL and the lap counter climbs. Then the phone comes up, the search finds a verified free spot, and the car parks. No fourth lap.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: A yellow car circles the real Esplanade streets past red FULL markers. Third lap. Still no parking.

scenes.title: Search
scenes.text: The phone rises, "Esplanade" is typed and the map flies to the area.

scenes.title: Filters
scenes.text: Pins drop. Tap 4-Wheeler, Free only and Verified, and the list narrows to two spots.

scenes.title: Before you go
scenes.text: A verified, free spot opens: its status, the vehicle types it takes and Get Directions.

scenes.title: Parked
scenes.text: The route draws on the map, the car drives straight there and parks.

scenes.title: Add a spot
scenes.text: The community form: name, area, vehicle type and a pin, then Submit. Know a spot? Add it for Kolkata.

craft: The map is real OpenStreetMap data of Esplanade, so local viewers recognise the streets in the first second.
Every screen is the live app: the search, the filter chips, the spot sheet and the Add Spot form.
Cut as two masters, 16:9 and 9:16, from one edit, at 120 BPM with no voiceover.
The story was built to run longer than our usual 25 seconds because the client wanted the full feature list included.

projects.title: WittyWing
projects.brief: A Chrome extension that adds tone-picked AI reply suggestions inside X's own reply box.
projects.approach: Everyone on X has typed "Congrats!" and deleted it. We start on that moment, then show the extension working inside the real reply dialog.

story.challenge: WittyWing lives in a reply box. The product is small, fast and easy to undersell, and the video had to make a Chrome extension feel like a relief rather than a gimmick, for people who already spend too long on X.
story.audience: Founders, indie hackers and creators who build in public and want to keep up with replies without losing hours on X.
story.idea: Open on the moment everyone on X knows: a friend's launch tweet, and a reply box where you type "Congrats!", delete it, try again and delete that too. Then WittyWing appears inside the same box and the whole flow, from tone to posted reply, takes under five seconds.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: A founder's launch tweet. "Congrats!" is typed and deleted, then "Huge, well done" too. Great tweet. Blank reply box.

scenes.title: The reveal
scenes.text: A paper wipe to WittyWing's site hero: Turn Every Tweet Into a Conversation.

scenes.title: The demo
scenes.text: Back in X, the toolbar appears under the reply box. Funny, Generate, copied, pasted, posted.

scenes.title: Eight tones
scenes.text: The site's tone grid lands card by card, then a gold highlight walks through all eight.

scenes.title: Built for builders
scenes.text: Six feature rows tick in: lives in X's reply box, sounds like you, never posts without permission.

scenes.title: Early users
scenes.text: A real early user's testimonial, with a marker sweep across "cut that time in half".

craft: X's reply dialog is recreated in its own dark theme, so the product shows up exactly where users will meet it.
The tweet and the generated reply are the site's own demo copy, and the testimonial is real.
Styled from WittyWing's own editorial identity: Playfair italics, mono labels, paper grain and an offset gold shadow.
Cut to a 100 BPM score, so the typing and deleting in the hook have room to land.

projects.title: GST Reco Pro
projects.brief: A browser tool that converts GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B PDFs into Excel locally, for chartered accountants and tax teams.
projects.approach: We open on the pain every CA knows (a pasted table landing in column A) and fix it with the tool's real batch flow.

story.challenge: Chartered accountants have seen every "AI-powered GST automation" pitch. GST Reco Pro's real edge is narrower and stronger: batch conversion of returns to Excel, without client data ever leaving the machine. The film had to say exactly that, precisely, in about 20 seconds.
story.audience: Chartered accountants, articles and corporate tax teams in India who live in GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B every filing season.
story.idea: Start with the pain every CA knows: copy a GSTR-3B table out of the PDF, paste it into Excel, and watch everything land in column A. Then drop 24 returns into the tool and show the same numbers arriving in their own columns.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: A GSTR-3B table is copied and pasted into Excel, lands in column A, and the cells flash red.

scenes.title: The reveal
scenes.text: The logo bars stack in: From PDF to Perfect Excel.

scenes.title: 24 returns at once
scenes.text: A stack of 24 PDFs drops into the real tool. Files Queued counts up and processing starts.

scenes.title: The result
scenes.text: The workbook fills month by month, the same numbers from the hook now each in its own column.

scenes.title: Zero data risk
scenes.text: The site's dark panel: data never leaves your machine, and zero uploads to servers.

craft: The hook's PDF is recreated from a real GSTR-3B the client supplied, with the business's identifying details blurred.
The result uses the client's own export layout, so CAs see the exact workbook they'll get.
A polished, precise tone in the site's own colours and type, with no voiceover and a quiet 120 BPM score.
Delivered in 16:9 for LinkedIn and YouTube, and 1:1 for feeds.

films.title: TDS Challan to Excel
films.brief: GST Reco Pro's TDS challan tool converts ITNS 281 and the new section-wise ITNS 281N challan receipts into one Excel workbook, up to 1,000 at a time, in the browser.
films.approach: Built as a companion to the GSTR film: the same column A pain, then one receipt flips from the old format to the new one and a mixed batch becomes a two-sheet workbook.

story.challenge: The new Income Tax Act brings a new challan format, so CAs now juggle two kinds of receipt. The film had to show that the tool reads both, in one batch, and what the workbook looks like, while matching the first GST Reco Pro film so the two read as a series.
story.audience: Chartered accountants, articles and corporate tax teams in India who reconcile TDS payments challan by challan.
story.idea: Same studio, new form. The hook repeats the GSTR film's paste-into-column-A pain with a 281N receipt, then a single receipt flips over like a card, legacy ITNS 281 on the front and the new ITNS 281N on the back.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: A 281N challan's section table is copied into Excel and every line lands in column A.

scenes.title: The tool
scenes.text: Precision Conversion Engine: TDS Challan PDF to Excel.

scenes.title: Both kinds
scenes.text: One receipt flips from ITNS 281 to ITNS 281N, then both sit side by side, auto-detected.

scenes.title: A mixed batch
scenes.text: A stack of both formats drops into the real tool. Files Queued counts up and processing starts.

scenes.title: Sheet 1
scenes.text: The Monthly Summary fills April to March, with the total.

scenes.title: Sheet 2
scenes.text: A click on the Challan-Wise Breakup tab: every challan line by line, each 281N code beside its old 1961-Act section.

scenes.title: Zero data risk
scenes.text: The site's dark panel: it all runs in the browser, so client data never leaves the machine.

scenes.title: Start free
scenes.text: The logo and gstrecopro.in.

craft: The receipts are recreated from real ITNS 281 and 281N challans, with identifying details blurred.
The workbook copies the tool's real export: its Monthly Summary and Challan-Wise Breakup sheets, headers and colours.
The GSTR film's identity carried over: the site's cream and orange, Hanken Grotesk and the three-bar mark, with the same 120 BPM score and a paper flip on the card turn.
Delivered in 16:9 and 1:1, like the first film. No voiceover.

projects.title: Faceiom
projects.brief: An Android app that reads one selfie and gives skin and face insights, plus product, routine, haircut and eyewear picks.
projects.approach: An overflowing bathroom shelf and a phone full of contradictory advice, cut down to one clear report and three products.

story.challenge: Skincare apps all promise to "analyse your skin". Faceiom's difference is what comes after: a short list of what to actually use, plus frames and haircuts for your face. The video had to sell that payoff on a phone screen, as an install ad, without making medical claims.
story.audience: Young adults buried in skincare advice and products, or unsure which glasses or haircut suit them.
story.idea: Ananya stands at a bathroom mirror in front of a shelf overflowing with products while contradictory advice bursts out of her phone. One selfie later, the clutter tumbles off the shelf and three products are left standing. Three products. Not thirty.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: An overflowing shelf and advice bubbles everywhere: "Double cleanse!", "Never use oils!". What does my skin need?

scenes.title: One selfie
scenes.text: Push into her phone: the upload screen, her face in the viewfinder, tap.

scenes.title: The scan
scenes.text: A mesh sweeps over her face as labels pop up: face shape, eyes, nose, skin type.

scenes.title: The results
scenes.text: Skin Score and Beauty Score rings fill, and the AI summary types itself in.

scenes.title: The picks
scenes.text: Visible concerns, then three recommended products for her skin type.

scenes.title: Three, not thirty
scenes.text: Back at the mirror, the clutter falls away. Cleanser, moisturiser and sunscreen stay.

scenes.title: Frames for your face
scenes.text: Rohan can't choose glasses. Faceiom maps his face and the right frames snap on.

scenes.title: Track progress
scenes.text: Report history and a progression line: track your skin journey.

craft: The app screens are recreated from the Play Store listing's own screenshots, so viewers see exactly what they'll install.
Two characters drawn in code carry the story, one for skin and one for style.
Made vertical-first at 9:16 for Reels, Shorts and app-install ads, cut to 120 BPM.
Ends on the app's own disclaimer: cosmetic insights, not a medical diagnosis.

projects.title: Sofi
projects.brief: A card collecting and battling game bot that lives in your Discord server.
projects.approach: A real-looking Discord channel. Three cards slam into chat within the first 1.5 seconds, and the fastest grab wins.

story.challenge: Sofi is a game that happens entirely inside Discord chat. Anyone who has played gets it instantly; anyone who hasn't needs to see the loop. The reel had to show the whole game in 20 seconds and earn the scroll-stop in the first one.
story.audience: Discord communities and anime, K-pop and gaming fans who would add a card game to their server.
story.idea: No intro, no logo first. A real-looking Discord channel, "sd" typed, and three cards slam into chat inside the first second and a half. Grab one, make it yours, then show how many people are already doing the same.

scenes.title: The drop
scenes.text: "sd" is typed in a Discord channel and three cards drop into chat.

scenes.title: The grab
scenes.text: Tap a number and the camera pushes in on the card. Fastest grab keeps it.

scenes.title: Make it yours
scenes.text: Frames cycle, from a library of over 600,000, then glows and backgrounds.

scenes.title: The scale
scenes.text: Sofi's own numbers count up: 28 million users and 265,571 servers.

craft: Discord's dark UI recreated to the pixel, so the drop reads as real chat.
The drop message and its 1, 2, 3 buttons match Sofi's own guide exactly.
Stats are taken live from sofi.gg on the day the reel was made.
Two masters, 9:16 for Reels, TikTok and Shorts and 4:5 for feeds, in Sofi's lavender and cyan.

projects.title: solAcc
projects.logline: Practise the OA you're actually facing.
projects.brief: A practice desk for company online assessments: timed puzzles, MCQs, coding and communication rounds, laid out company by company.
projects.approach: A week out from placement season: pick the company, then drill its real rounds, including the gamified puzzles nobody else lets you practise.

story.challenge: Placement-season students are flooded with question banks. solAcc's difference is that it's laid out company by company, including the game-based puzzle rounds nobody else lets you drill. The promo had to make a student feel that difference a week before their online assessment.
story.audience: Indian engineering students in placement season (CSE, IT, ECE, EE and mechanical) a week away from a company's online assessment.
story.idea: Open on the pain of the game-based round: the Key Maze, where the walls aren't drawn. The arrow hits a wall you can't see and you're sent back to the start. Then tour the desk built for that company, and come back to the same maze to clear it.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: The Key Maze: the arrow hits an invisible wall, the cell flashes pink and you're back at the start. Walls you can't see.

scenes.title: The reveal
scenes.text: The solAcc wordmark: a practice desk for company OAs.

scenes.title: 39 companies
scenes.text: The company table. Accenture gets bookmarked and slides into Saved.

scenes.title: Not just DSA
scenes.text: Practice-focus rows light up for VLSI, embedded, electrical, mechanical and low-level design.

scenes.title: One desk
scenes.text: The Accenture desk: OA puzzles, MCQs, coding lab and communication, one click each.

scenes.title: The maze, cleared
scenes.text: The same maze again. Three keys collected, exit reached, with time to spare.

scenes.title: MCQs by topic
scenes.text: A real pseudocode question, answered and marked attempted.

scenes.title: Code and run
scenes.text: Python typed into Code Studio, Run, and both test cases pass.

scenes.title: Unlock every set
scenes.text: Free and paid side by side: start free, then one unlock for every question, with ₹40 off for a partner-college email.

craft: Every screen, question and coding problem is solAcc's real content, captured from the live site.
A small story arc: you fail the maze in the hook and clear it later in the film.
Built in the site's own dark sage palette and its Satoshi typeface.
Cut to 120 BPM with no voiceover, one feature per shot.

projects.title: DBT Invoice Extractor
projects.brief: A web app that reads invoices with AI, lets finance teams verify every field and the totals, then files them with a full audit trail.
projects.approach: The old way fails on a single transposed number. The app's per-field confidence scores and live cross-check catch it before anything gets filed.

story.challenge: Invoice extraction tools all claim AI accuracy. For a finance team, the question is whether they can trust the numbers before approving them. The launch film had to show that trust being built, field by field and total by total, for an audience that's sceptical by profession.
story.audience: Accounts payable and finance teams, and project accountants who file invoices against projects and vendors.
story.idea: Open on the old way failing: someone keys an invoice into a spreadsheet and transposes two digits, and the cell flashes red. Then follow one invoice through the product, from upload to a Balanced cross-check, an approval and an audit trail.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: An invoice keyed into a spreadsheet, two digits transposed, the total flashes red.

scenes.title: The reveal
scenes.text: The DBT Invoice Extractor lockup on navy: read, verify, approve and file.

scenes.title: Upload
scenes.text: The invoice is dropped into the ingestion page and extraction starts.

scenes.title: Verify
scenes.text: A scan passes over the document as each field fills in with its own confidence score.

scenes.title: Cross-check
scenes.text: Line items plus tax are checked against the declared total. Balanced. Approve and file.

scenes.title: Analytics
scenes.text: Spend by project and vendor, and a payables horizon of what's due when.

scenes.title: Audit trail
scenes.text: New rows slide into the immutable audit log.

craft: Every screen is captured from the real app and rebuilt shot for shot in its own light slate UI.
The invoice, vendor and amounts are illustrative. No accuracy or speed figures are claimed, because the workspace was a test one.
A polished, precise tone on a navy stage, with the logo's orange used sparingly for highlights.
Cut to 120 BPM with cuts on the beat. No voiceover.

projects.title: BOS
projects.logline: One product record, from pack to pitch.
projects.brief: An internal workspace for product knowledge, competitor intel and sales enablement, with approvals and a cited AI assistant.
projects.approach: A dashboard that builds itself, then one product record followed through every role: create, approve, compare, pitch, ask.

story.challenge: BOS is an internal tool, so this isn't an ad. It's a tutorial its own staff would actually watch. It had to show five roles and a full product lifecycle in under 40 seconds, and leave people knowing where to click.
story.audience: Product managers, product owners and sales teams at AAA Bed who use BOS every day.
story.idea: Follow one real product, Biscamix Choco, through the whole documented lifecycle, from pack artwork to a sales pitch, in five numbered steps. The cursor clicks the real sidebar every time, so the tour doubles as a map of the app.

scenes.title: The promise
scenes.text: A dashboard builds itself, then the promise: new product to sales pitch in 5 steps.

scenes.title: Step 1: create
scenes.text: The Biscamix Choco pack is dropped onto Scan product and the code, barcode and names fill in.

scenes.title: Step 2: approve
scenes.text: The product owner approves. It's published, indexed for the AI Assistant and logged.

scenes.title: Step 3: compare
scenes.text: Two products side by side, with the differentiator highlighted.

scenes.title: Step 4: the pitch
scenes.text: Pick the buyer, cafés, and a positioning statement types itself out, with citations.

scenes.title: Step 5: ask
scenes.text: A question to the AI Assistant, answered from the published record and cited.

craft: Every screen is the real BOS app, captured logged in, and the product is a real SKU with its own pack artwork.
The steps follow BOS's own documentation of each role's journey, so the video matches the training material.
Calm and confident rather than salesy: a clean walkthrough in the app's dark theme.
Cut to 120 BPM with no voiceover, so it can be shared and watched with the sound off.

projects.title: ProMed United
projects.brief: Physician-led medical education, from premed and the MCAT through boards, the Match and intern year.
projects.approach: A drawn premed student faces a giant tangled scribble between first science class and first patient, and the path straightens out stage by stage.

story.challenge: Medical education is a long, confusing road: MCAT, med school, research, boards, the Match, intern year. ProMed United's promise is one clearer path with a physician beside you. The film had to make that journey feel lighter in about 25 seconds.
story.audience: Premeds and medical students facing the long road from MCAT to the Match, who want a plan and a mentor.
story.idea: A premed student faces a giant tangled scribble between "first science class" and "first patient", tagged with every exam on the way. Then the knot pulls straight into one blue path, a mentor walks in beside her, and she changes from hoodie to white coat to scrubs as she passes each gate.

scenes.title: The knot
scenes.text: Night. A tangled scribble between first science class and first patient, tagged MCAT, USMLE, COMLEX, the Match. Medicine is a long journey.

scenes.title: A clearer path
scenes.text: The knot pulls straight into a blue path, day breaks and the mentor walks in. Big ambitions. A clearer path.

scenes.title: Med School Launchpad
scenes.text: An MCAT practice question with its explanation, then through the Med School gate into a white coat.

scenes.title: Research Accelerator
scenes.text: At the lab bench, a 16-week research path and a forest plot drawing itself.

scenes.title: Study together
scenes.text: Late night: a study channel full of classmates and live mentor office hours.

scenes.title: Intern Bootcamp
scenes.text: In scrubs at a patient's bedside, the patient journey ticks from the ED to the first follow-up.

craft: The student, the mentor, classmates and a patient are all drawn and rigged in code, with costume changes at each gate.
Every headline is ProMed United's own copy, and the hero is rebuilt from promedunited.com.
The classroom is behind a login, so its screens are recreated in the site's own design.
A hopeful 100 BPM score with day breaking on the reveal. No voiceover.

projects.title: GitHub
projects.brief: The developer platform pitched as the whole loop in one place: issues, an AI agent's fix, a cloud dev environment, CI, security and the merge.
projects.approach: A cursor assigns an issue to the coding agent, and within three seconds a draft PR appears. The rest of the loop runs at the same pace.

story.challenge: A concept piece: could the same pipeline make a convincing launch-style film for one of the most familiar products in software? Developers know GitHub's interface by heart, so every screen had to feel exactly right.
story.audience: Shipping developers who want flow, green CI and no secrets leaking into the repo.
story.idea: Follow one bug from issue to merge without leaving GitHub. Assign the issue to Copilot, and a few seconds later a draft pull request appears. Then Codespaces, Actions, push protection and the merge, one product per shot.

scenes.title: Assign the issue
scenes.text: Issue #482 is assigned to Copilot, and a draft pull request appears in the timeline.

scenes.title: The reveal
scenes.text: The Invertocat over GitHub's own headline: The future of building happens together.

scenes.title: Copilot
scenes.text: The agent session ticks through its steps alongside the diff that fixes the bug.

scenes.title: Codespaces
scenes.text: A codespace spins up, npm test runs and three tests pass.

scenes.title: Actions
scenes.text: Matrix builds on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows go green. All checks have passed.

scenes.title: Push protection
scenes.text: A git push carrying a secret is declined, next to GitHub's own figure of 8.3M leaks stopped.

scenes.title: Merged
scenes.text: Merge pull request, confirm, and the issue closes itself.

craft: Every headline is GitHub's own copy, and the stat is taken from github.com on the day it was made.
GitHub's dark UI rebuilt in its own colours and typeface, with Mona Sans and mono uppercase eyebrows.
The repository, issue, code and the leaked key are invented. The key is fake and masked.
Cut to a 120 BPM electronic score, one product per shot.

projects.title: Techolution
projects.brief: Outcome-backed enterprise automation, pitched to the leaders who sign off on AI budgets.
projects.approach: We frame it around the CFO's risk, then answer with the company's published outcomes and guarantee.

story.challenge: Enterprise AI is a crowded pitch, and the person who signs off carries the risk. Techolution's own positioning is accountability: outcome-backed AI with a money-back challenge. The film had to put that in front of a CFO without a boardroom full of buzzwords.
story.audience: Enterprise leaders who sign off on AI budgets and carry the risk, above all the CFO.
story.idea: A boardroom where three department heads slide AI pilot folders at the CFO, and the pile keeps growing. She does her due diligence: she takes the site's own profitability quiz, then follows three real Techolution case studies floor by floor, each with its own character, before signing up for the money-back challenge.

scenes.title: The hook
scenes.text: Department heads slide AI pilot folders across the table. Everyone wants the budget. Nobody wants the accountability.

scenes.title: The quiz
scenes.text: The CFO takes the site's own profitability quiz, clicks past 100% and builds her roadmap.

scenes.title: Value Finder
scenes.text: A plant director's wall of 30+ AI ideas narrows to five high-ROI projects.

scenes.title: Learns on the job
scenes.text: A media scheduler overrides a slot and the AI asks to learn from it. Yes, learn this.

scenes.title: Roadside help
scenes.text: A driver on the hard shoulder finds roadside assistance instantly through the AI assistant.

scenes.title: The 100K Challenge
scenes.text: The CFO signs: invest $100k, Techolution multiplies it with BPA 4.0, and delivers at least 2x ROI in 100 days or your money back.

scenes.title: Full Enterprise Automation
scenes.text: The feature board: the BPA 4.0 components and services, with the whole cast along the bottom.

craft: Every claim and case figure is from techolution.com, captured on the day it was made.
Flat illustrated characters for each case on the site's light blue-grid world, all drawn in code.
The quiz, the Value Finder and the Teach Me panel are rebuilt from the site's own interface.
A 56-second B2B story cut to 120 BPM in a minor key, with no voiceover.
